chapter.name: Playing with Constructions
hard_words: compass (define it: a tool that draws circles of a set radius)
radius (define it: distance from the centre to the circle)
diagonal (define it: a line joining opposite corners)
equidistant (say: the same distance from both)

source: Why a hand cannot draw a perfect circle
videos.note: The chapter opener: artwork made only from straight lines and circles, and the question of how it could be drawn exactly, left open.

source: Look at five artwork pictures: two circles of the same size

items.question: Look at five artwork pictures: two circles of the same size side by side and touching; two circles one inside the other with the same centre (the inner one about half the size of the outer); three equal circles in a row, each overlapping the next; a mouse face (one big circle for the face, two smaller circles for the ears, two small circles with dots for the eyes, a dot for the nose and a short line for the mouth); and two lines crossing like an X with a small circle at the bottom end of each line. Try drawing them freehand.
steps: Look at each picture and spot the circles in it.
Sketch the circles in the right places and sizes.
Compare your freehand circles with the pictures and see how round they are.
items.answer: Open ended. A correct drawing uses round circles of the sizes and positions described. Freehand circles are usually uneven, which is why a compass is introduced next.

videos.answer: Open ended. A correct drawing uses round circles of the sizes and positions described. Freehand circles are usually uneven, which is why a compass is introduced next.

source: Mark a point P in your notebook. Then mark as many points as

items.question: Mark a point P in your notebook. Then mark as many points as possible, in different directions, that are 4 cm away from P.
steps: Mark P in the middle of the page.
Place the ruler with 0 cm at P and mark a point at 4 cm.
Turn the ruler to another direction and mark another point at 4 cm from P; repeat in many directions.
Notice the points form a round shape around P.
items.answer: All the points you mark lie on a round curve around P, each exactly 4 cm from P. With enough points they join into a circle of radius 4 cm.

videos.answer: All the points you mark lie on a round curve around P, each exactly 4 cm from P. With enough points they join into a circle of radius 4 cm.

source: Imagine marking all the points that are 4 cm away from the p

items.question: Imagine marking all the points that are 4 cm away from the point P. How would they look?
steps: Every point is the same distance, 4 cm, from P.
Joining all such points gives a perfectly round curve.
This curve is a circle with centre P.
items.answer: They would form a circle with centre P and radius 4 cm.

videos.answer: They would form a circle with centre P and radius 4 cm.

source: How can a compass be used to mark points that are 4 cm from

items.question: How can a compass be used to mark points that are 4 cm from P?
steps: Place the compass next to a ruler and open it until the tip and the pencil point are 4 cm apart.
Put the tip firmly on P.
Keep the tip fixed and move only the pencil all the way round.
items.answer: Open the compass so that the distance between its tip and the pencil is 4 cm (check against a ruler). Fix the tip at P and swing the pencil; every point it marks is 4 cm from P, giving a full circle.

videos.answer: Open the compass so that the distance between its tip and the pencil is 4 cm (check against a ruler). Fix the tip at P and swing the pencil; every point it marks is 4 cm from P, giving a full circle.

source: Take a point on the circle drawn with centre P and radius 4

items.question: Take a point on the circle drawn with centre P and radius 4 cm. Is its distance from P equal to 4 cm, less than 4 cm or greater than 4 cm? What about any other point on the circle?
steps: The pencil stayed exactly 4 cm from the tip all the time.
So every point on the circle is 4 cm from P.
This fixed distance is the radius; P is the centre.
items.answer: Equal to 4 cm for every point on the circle. P is called the centre and the distance from the centre to any point on the circle is called the radius.

videos.answer: Equal to 4 cm for every point on the circle. P is called the centre and the distance from the centre to any point on the circle is called the radius.

source: Activity (section 8.1)

items.question: Using a ruler and a compass, recreate the artwork pictures: two touching circles, two circles with the same centre, three overlapping circles, the mouse face, and the X with two small circles. Try to make them look as good as the book's pictures.
steps: Choose a radius and set the compass with the ruler.
Fix the tip at each centre and draw each circle.
For concentric circles, keep the same tip point and change the radius.
Add the dots and lines with a ruler.
items.answer: Open ended. Correct drawings: touching circles have centres at a distance of twice the radius; concentric circles share one centre but have different radii; overlapping circles have centres closer than twice the radius; the mouse face has all its circles drawn with a compass.

videos.answer: Open ended. Correct drawings: touching circles have centres at a distance of twice the radius; concentric circles share one centre but have different radii; overlapping circles have centres closer than twice the radius; the mouse face has all its circles drawn with a compass.

source: Construct this wave: a central straight line AB = 8 cm. The

items.question: Construct this wave: a central straight line AB = 8 cm. The first wave is a half circle on the left half of AB lying above the line (A to X), and the second wave is a half circle on the right half lying below the line (X to B). Both half circles are shaded with vertical lines.
steps: Draw AB = 8 cm with a ruler.
Mark X on AB at 4 cm from A.
Set the compass to 2 cm; put the tip at the point 2 cm from A and draw a half circle above AB from A to X.
Put the tip at the point 6 cm from A (2 cm from B) and draw a half circle below AB from X to B.
Shade both half circles with vertical lines.
items.answer: AB = 8 cm, AX = XB = 4 cm. Each half circle has diameter 4 cm, so radius 2 cm. First half circle: tip at the point 2 cm from A on AB, drawn above the line. Second half circle: tip at the point 6 cm from A on AB, drawn below the line.

videos.answer: AB = 8 cm, AX = XB = 4 cm. Each half circle has diameter 4 cm, so radius 2 cm. First half circle: tip at the point 2 cm from A on AB, drawn above the line. Second half circle: tip at the point 6 cm from A on AB, drawn below the line.

source: Figure it Out Q1 (section 8.1)

items.question: In the wave with a central line AB = 8 cm, the first wave is a half circle from A to X on the line AB. What radius should be taken in the compass to get this half circle? What should be the length of AX? a) What radius should be taken in the compass? b) What should be the length of AX?
steps: The two equal half circles share the 8 cm line, so AX is 8 cm divided by 2, which gives 4 cm.
AX is the diameter of the half circle.
Radius = 4 cm ÷ 2 = 2 cm.
items.answer: a) 2 cm, b) AX = 4 cm

videos.answer: a) 2 cm, b) AX = 4 cm

source: Figure it Out Q2 (section 8.1)

items.question: Take a central line of a different length and try to draw the wave on it.
steps: Draw a line AB of any length L.
Mark the middle point X.
Set the compass to L ÷ 4 and draw the first half circle above AB from A to X.
Draw the second half circle below AB from X to B with the same radius.
items.answer: Open ended. For a central line of length L, each half circle has diameter L ÷ 2 and radius L ÷ 4. Example: L = 10 cm gives two half circles of diameter 5 cm and radius 2.5 cm; L = 12 cm gives radius 3 cm.

videos.answer: Open ended. For a central line of length L, each half circle has diameter L ÷ 2 and radius L ÷ 4. Example: L = 10 cm gives two half circles of diameter 5 cm and radius 2.5 cm; L = 12 cm gives radius 3 cm.

source: Draw a person made of a circle for the head, a short straigh

items.question: Draw a person made of a circle for the head, a short straight neck line below it, and a body that is a rectangle whose top edge is a curved arc dipping in the middle. How will you draw the curved top of the body with a compass? Where should the tip be placed and what radius should be used?
steps: Draw the head circle with the compass.
Draw the neck as a short vertical line below the circle.
Draw the body as a rectangle without the top edge: two vertical sides and a flat bottom.
Fix a radius and try the tip at different spots above the body until the arc from one top corner to the other touches the bottom of the neck line.
Draw the arc and rub out the trial marks.
items.answer: Open ended. The head is a circle. The body is a rectangle with vertical sides and a flat bottom, and its top is an arc of a circle joining the two top corners and dipping down in the middle. The compass tip goes above the body (outside it, on the line through the middle of the body) at a point found by trial, and the radius is the distance from that tip to the top corners. The neck line joins the bottom of the head to the lowest point of the arc.

videos.answer: Open ended. The head is a circle. The body is a rectangle with vertical sides and a flat bottom, and its top is an arc of a circle joining the two top corners and dipping down in the middle. The compass tip goes above the body (outside it, on the line through the middle of the body) at a point found by trial, and the radius is the distance from that tip to the top corners. The neck line joins the bottom of the head to the lowest point of the arc.

source: How do you draw these eyes with a compass? Each eye is an al

items.question: How do you draw these eyes with a compass? Each eye is an almond shape made of an upper curve and a lower curve meeting at two pointed corners, with a filled dark circle (pupil) in the middle. The two eyes sit side by side and are identical.
steps: Draw two light horizontal guide lines (supporting lines) that help to place the compass tips.
Choose a radius and place the tip at B to draw the upper curve between the two corners.
Place the tip at A, the same distance from the middle on the other side, and with the same radius draw the lower curve.
Fill the pupil circle in the middle.
Repeat for the second eye and adjust until both eyes are symmetrical and identical.
items.answer: Open ended. The upper and lower curves are arcs of equal radius. Their compass tips (points A and B) lie on the line through the middle of the eye, one on each side, equally far from the middle, so that the eye is symmetrical. Draw a filled circle in the middle as the pupil.

videos.answer: Open ended. The upper and lower curves are arcs of equal radius. Their compass tips (points A and B) lie on the line through the middle of the eye, one on each side, equally far from the middle, so that the eye is symmetrical. Draw a filled circle in the middle as the pupil.

source: Figure it Out Q3, Try This (section 8.1)

items.question: Try to recreate the figure where the waves are smaller than a half circle (as appearing in the neck of the figure 'A Person'). The challenge here is to get both the waves to be identical. This may be tricky!
steps: Draw the central line and mark the chord for each wave.
Choose one radius bigger than half the chord.
For the upper arc, place the tip below the line on the perpendicular through the middle of the chord, at a fixed distance, and draw the arc above the line.
For the lower arc, place the tip above the line at the same distance from the line and use the same radius.
Check that both arcs look identical.
items.answer: Open ended. Both waves are arcs of the same radius on the same length of chord. A correct drawing shows two identical arcs, one above the line and one below the line, each shorter than a half circle.

videos.answer: Open ended. Both waves are arcs of the same radius on the same length of chord. A correct drawing shows two identical arcs, one above the line and one below the line, each shorter than a half circle.

source: What shapes are a rectangle and four small squares drawn in

items.question: What shapes are a rectangle and four small squares drawn in a group? What makes them squares and rectangles?
steps: Look at a rectangle: its opposite sides are equal and each corner is a right angle.
Look at a square: all four sides are equal and each corner is a right angle.
items.answer: A rectangle has two properties: R1) its opposite sides are equal in length, and R2) all its angles are 90°. A square has: S1) all its sides are equal, and S2) all its angles are 90°.

videos.answer: A rectangle has two properties: R1) its opposite sides are equal in length, and R2) all its angles are 90°. A square has: S1) all its sides are equal, and S2) all its angles are 90°.

source: A rectangle ABCD has corners A (top left), B (top right), C

items.question: A rectangle ABCD has corners A (top left), B (top right), C (bottom right), D (bottom left). Besides ABCD it can be named BCDA, CDAB, DABC, ADCB, DCBA, CBAD and BADC. Can a rectangle be named using any combination of the labels around its corners? What names are allowed and what names are not?
steps: Check that each pair of letters next to each other in the name is a side of the rectangle.
ABDC fails because B to D is a diagonal, not a side.
So go round the rectangle one corner after another.
items.answer: No. ABDC and ACBD are not allowed. In a valid name the corners come in order, going round the rectangle, starting from any corner and going in either direction.

videos.answer: No. ABDC and ACBD are not allowed. In a valid name the corners come in order, going round the rectangle, starting from any corner and going in either direction.

source: Which of the following is not a name for this square? The sq

items.question: Which of the following is not a name for this square? The square has corners S (top left), P (top right), Q (bottom right) and R (bottom left). 1. PQSR 2. SPQR 3. RSPQ 4. QRSP 1) PQSR 2) SPQR 3) RSPQ 4) QRSP
steps: Going round the square the corners come in the order S, P, Q, R.
SPQR, RSPQ and QRSP follow this order.
PQSR goes from Q to S, which is a diagonal, so it is not a valid name.
items.answer: PQSR

videos.answer: PQSR

source: Figure it Out Q2 (section 8.2)

items.question: Identify if there are any squares in this collection. Use measurements if needed. On a dot grid there are four tilted 4-sided figures with corners on dots: A is a diamond whose left to right span equals its top to bottom span (about 8 dots each way); B is a diamond about 6 dots wide and 8 dots tall; C is a diamond about 10 dots wide and 8 dots tall; D is a small tilted long rectangle.
steps: A square needs 4 equal sides and 4 angles of 90°.
A has equal width and height, so its sides and angles are equal: a square.
B and C have unequal widths and heights, so they are diamonds whose angles are not 90°.
D has two long and two short sides, so it is a rectangle, not a square.
items.answer: A is a square.

videos.answer: A is a square.

source: A square piece of paper has all its sides equal and all angl

items.question: A square piece of paper has all its sides equal and all angles 90°. It is rotated (tilted so it looks like a diamond). Is it still a square? Are all the sides still equal? Are all the angles still 90°?
steps: Rotating does not change lengths.
Rotating does not change angles.
So both square properties S1 and S2 still hold.
items.answer: Yes, it is still a square. All the sides are still equal and all the angles are still 90°, because rotating a square does not change its lengths and angles. In the same way a rotated rectangle is still a rectangle.

videos.answer: Yes, it is still a square. All the sides are still equal and all the angles are still 90°, because rotating a square does not change its lengths and angles. In the same way a rotated rectangle is still a rectangle.

source: Is it possible to reason out if the sides are equal or not,

items.question: Is it possible to reason out if the sides are equal or not, and if the angles are right or not, without using any measuring instruments in the above figure? Can we do this by only looking at the position of corners in the dot grid?
steps: Count how many dots across and how many down it takes to go from one corner to the next.
If every side uses the same counts, the sides are equal.
If the next side uses the counts swapped for a turn (across and down exchanged), the angle is 90°.
items.answer: Yes. The positions of the dots make it possible. Moving from one corner to the next by the same number of dots across and down, and turning with the counts swapped, gives equal sides and right angles.

videos.answer: Yes. The positions of the dots make it possible. Moving from one corner to the next by the same number of dots across and down, and turning with the counts swapped, gives equal sides and right angles.

source: Figure it Out Q1 (section 8.2)

items.question: Draw the rectangle and four squares configuration (a rectangle in the middle, about twice as wide as tall, with four equal small squares placed near its four corners, one outside each corner, not touching it) on a dot paper. What did you do to recreate this figure so that the four squares are placed symmetrically around the rectangle? Discuss with your classmates.
steps: Draw the rectangle on dots, counting dots along each side.
From each corner of the rectangle, move one dot diagonally outwards (same count each time).
Draw an equal square at each of the four places, counting the same number of dots for every square.
Use the same counts on the left and right, top and bottom so the figure is symmetrical.
items.answer: Open ended. A correct drawing shows a rectangle with four equal squares around it placed in the same way at each corner. Book hint: draw the rectangle and then leave one dot distance diagonally to place the four smaller squares.

videos.answer: Open ended. A correct drawing shows a rectangle with four equal squares around it placed in the same way at each corner. Book hint: draw the rectangle and then leave one dot distance diagonally to place the four smaller squares.

source: Figure it Out Q3 (section 8.2)

items.question: Draw at least 3 rotated squares and rectangles on a dot grid. Draw them such that their corners are on the dots. Verify if the squares and rectangles that you have drawn satisfy their respective properties.
steps: Pick dots as corners so that each side goes the same number of dots across and down for a square.
Join the corners with a ruler.
Measure the sides with the ruler.
Check the angles with a protractor or a set square.
items.answer: Open ended. A correct drawing: each rotated square has 4 equal sides and 4 angles of 90°; each rotated rectangle has equal opposite sides and 4 angles of 90°. For example a diamond with corners 4 dots up, 4 dots right, 4 dots down and 4 dots left of its centre is a square.

videos.answer: Open ended. A correct drawing: each rotated square has 4 equal sides and 4 angles of 90°; each rotated rectangle has equal opposite sides and 4 angles of 90°. For example a diamond with corners 4 dots up, 4 dots right, 4 dots down and 4 dots left of its centre is a square.

source: How would you construct a square with a side of 6 cm? A squa

items.question: How would you construct a square with a side of 6 cm? A square PQRS of side length 6 cm is constructed.
steps: Draw PQ = 6 cm with a ruler.
Place the protractor with its centre at P and its baseline along PQ, mark 90° and draw a perpendicular through P.
Mark S on this perpendicular so that PS = 6 cm (ruler), or open the compass to 6 cm, tip at P, and mark an arc.
At Q draw the perpendicular to PQ and mark R with QR = 6 cm (with the compass: keep the radius at 6 cm and put the tip at Q).
Join R and S. Check RS = 6 cm, ∠R = 90°, ∠S = 90°.
items.answer: Square PQRS with PQ = QR = RS = SP = 6 cm and all angles 90°. RS = 6 cm and ∠R = ∠S = 90°.

videos.answer: Square PQRS with PQ = QR = RS = SP = 6 cm and all angles 90°. RS = 6 cm and ∠R = ∠S = 90°.

source: In the construction of square PQRS with PQ = 6 cm, can you s

items.question: In the construction of square PQRS with PQ = 6 cm, can you see why PS should be 6 cm long?
steps: Property S1: all sides of a square are equal.
PQ = 6 cm, so PS = 6 cm.
items.answer: Because all the sides of a square are equal, so PS must be the same length as PQ, which is 6 cm.

videos.answer: Because all the sides of a square are equal, so PS must be the same length as PQ, which is 6 cm.

source: In the square PQRS of side 6 cm just constructed, how long i

items.question: In the square PQRS of side 6 cm just constructed, how long is the side RS and what are the measures of ∠R and ∠S?
steps: All sides of a square are equal, so RS = 6 cm.
All angles of a square are 90°, so ∠R = ∠S = 90°.

source: Is it possible to construct a 4-sided figure in which all th

items.question: Is it possible to construct a 4-sided figure in which all the angles are equal to 90° but opposite sides are not equal?
steps: Draw one side and the two perpendiculars at its ends.
The two perpendiculars stay the same distance apart, so the opposite side is the same length as the first side.
So opposite sides are always equal.
items.answer: No. If all four angles are 90° the figure is a rectangle, so its opposite sides are equal.

videos.answer: No. If all four angles are 90° the figure is a rectangle, so its opposite sides are equal.

source: Construct Q1 (section 8.3)

items.question: Draw a rectangle with sides of length 4 cm and 6 cm. After drawing, check if it satisfies both the rectangle properties.
steps: Draw AB = 4 cm.
Draw perpendiculars at A and B.
Mark D on the one at A with AD = 6 cm and C on the one at B with BC = 6 cm.
Join D and C.
Measure: opposite sides are equal (4 and 4, 6 and 6) and all angles are 90°.
items.answer: Rectangle ABCD with AB = CD = 4 cm, AD = BC = 6 cm and ∠A = ∠B = ∠C = ∠D = 90°. Both properties hold.

videos.answer: Rectangle ABCD with AB = CD = 4 cm, AD = BC = 6 cm and ∠A = ∠B = ∠C = ∠D = 90°. Both properties hold.

source: Construct Q2 (section 8.3)

items.question: Draw a rectangle of sides 2 cm and 10 cm. After drawing, check if it satisfies both the rectangle properties.
steps: Draw PQ = 10 cm.
Draw perpendiculars at P and Q.
Mark S with PS = 2 cm and R with QR = 2 cm.
Join S and R.
Check that SR = 10 cm and all angles are 90°.
items.answer: Rectangle PQRS with PQ = SR = 10 cm, PS = QR = 2 cm and ∠P = ∠Q = ∠R = ∠S = 90°.

videos.answer: Rectangle PQRS with PQ = SR = 10 cm, PS = QR = 2 cm and ∠P = ∠Q = ∠R = ∠S = 90°.

source: Construct a rectangle ABCD with AB = 7 cm and BC = 4 cm.

items.question: Construct a rectangle ABCD with AB = 7 cm and BC = 4 cm.
steps: Draw AB = 7 cm.
Draw a perpendicular at A and mark D with AD = 4 cm.
Draw a perpendicular at B and mark C with BC = 4 cm.
Join D and C and check DC = 7 cm.
items.answer: Rectangle ABCD with AB = CD = 7 cm and BC = AD = 4 cm, all angles 90°.

videos.answer: Rectangle ABCD with AB = CD = 7 cm and BC = AD = 4 cm, all angles 90°.

source: In rectangle ABCD with AB = 7 cm and BC = 4 cm, X moves alon

items.question: In rectangle ABCD with AB = 7 cm and BC = 4 cm, X moves along side AD and Y moves along side BC. At which positions will the points X and Y be at their closest? When do you think they will be the farthest? What does your intuition say? Discuss with your classmates.
steps: Try several positions with a ruler.
XY is 7 cm whenever X and Y are at equal distances from A and B.
XY is longest when X and Y are at opposite corners.
items.answer: Closest: when X and Y are the same distance from A and B respectively (for example X = A and Y = B), where XY = 7 cm. Farthest: when X is at one corner and Y at the opposite corner (X = A and Y = C, or X = D and Y = B), where XY is a diagonal of about 8 cm 1 mm (√65 cm).

videos.answer: Closest: when X and Y are the same distance from A and B respectively (for example X = A and Y = B), where XY = 7 cm. Farthest: when X is at one corner and Y at the opposite corner (X = A and Y = C, or X = D and Y = B), where XY is a diagonal of about 8 cm 1 mm (√65 cm).

source: How does the minimum distance between the points X and Y com

items.question: How does the minimum distance between the points X and Y compare to the length of AB (7 cm)?
steps: Measure XY when X and Y are level (same distance from A and B).
You get 7 cm each time, which is the length of AB.
items.answer: The minimum distance of XY is 7 cm, which is equal to AB.

videos.answer: The minimum distance of XY is 7 cm, which is equal to AB.

source: Rectangle ABCD has AB = 7 cm, BC = 4 cm. Measure XY and fill

items.question: Rectangle ABCD has AB = 7 cm, BC = 4 cm. Measure XY and fill in: When X is 5 mm away from A and Y is 3 cm away from B, XY = __ cm __ mm. When X is 1 cm away from A and Y is 1 cm away from B, XY = __ cm __ mm. When X is 2 cm away from A and Y is 4 cm away from B, XY = __ cm __ mm. a) X is 5 mm from A and Y is 3 cm from B b) X is 1 cm from A and Y is 1 cm from B c) X is 2 cm from A and Y is 4 cm from B
steps: Across the rectangle the distance is 7 cm; the up and down difference between the two points changes.
a) the difference is 3 cm − 5 mm = 2.5 cm, XY = √(49 + 6.25) ≈ 7.4 cm.
b) the difference is 0, XY = 7 cm.
c) the difference is 4 cm − 2 cm = 2 cm, XY = √(49 + 4) ≈ 7.3 cm.
items.answer: a) 7 cm 4 mm, b) 7 cm 0 mm, c) 7 cm 3 mm

videos.answer: a) 7 cm 4 mm, b) 7 cm 0 mm, c) 7 cm 3 mm

source: Is there a shorthand way of writing it down? In all the sent

items.question: Is there a shorthand way of writing it down? In all the sentences, only the position of X, Y and the length XY changes. So we could write this as a table with columns: Distance of X from A, Distance of Y from B, Length of XY. Fill the table for the three cases above. 1) X from A: 5 mm, Y from B: 3 cm 2) X from A: 1 cm, Y from B: 1 cm 3) X from A: 2 cm, Y from B: 4 cm
steps: Write each case as a row.
Put the two distances and then the measured length XY.
items.answer: Rows: (5 mm, 3 cm, 7.4 cm), (1 cm, 1 cm, 7 cm), (2 cm, 4 cm, 7.3 cm).

videos.answer: Rows: (5 mm, 3 cm, 7.4 cm), (1 cm, 1 cm, 7 cm), (2 cm, 4 cm, 7.3 cm).

source: What happens to the length XY when X and Y are placed at the

items.question: What happens to the length XY when X and Y are placed at the same distance away from A and B, respectively? Fill the table: X from A is 5 mm and Y from B is 5 mm; X from A is 1 cm and Y from B is 1 cm; X from A is 1 cm 5 mm and Y from B is 1 cm 5 mm. 1) 5 mm and 5 mm 2) 1 cm and 1 cm 3) 1 cm 5 mm and 1 cm 5 mm
steps: Equal distances mean X and Y are at the same height.
So XY is parallel to AB and as long as AB: 7 cm.
items.answer: XY = 7 cm in every case, the same as AB.

videos.answer: XY = 7 cm in every case, the same as AB.

source: In each of these cases (X and Y at the same distance from A

items.question: In each of these cases (X and Y at the same distance from A and B), observe 1. how the length XY compares to that of AB and 2. the shape of the 4-sided figure ABYX. 1) How XY compares with AB 2) Shape of ABYX
steps: XY and AB are both 7 cm.
The four angles at A, B, Y and X are all 90° and opposite sides are equal, so ABYX is a rectangle.
items.answer: XY = AB; ABYX is a rectangle.

videos.answer: XY = AB; ABYX is a rectangle.

source: How does the farthest distance between X and Y compare with

items.question: How does the farthest distance between X and Y compare with the length of AC? BD? (AC and BD are the diagonals of rectangle ABCD with AB = 7 cm and BC = 4 cm.)
steps: The farthest is when X and Y are at opposite corners.
Then XY is exactly a diagonal, AC or BD.
items.answer: The farthest distance between X and Y is equal to AC or BD, which is about 8 cm 1 mm (√65 cm).

videos.answer: The farthest distance between X and Y is equal to AC or BD, which is about 8 cm 1 mm (√65 cm).

source: Construct a rectangle ACDF that can be divided into two iden

items.question: Construct a rectangle ACDF that can be divided into two identical squares ABEF and BCDE, with no measurements imposed. If AF is assigned 4 cm, what must the length of AC be?
steps: Draw a rough diagram: AB = BC and FE = ED, and all the short lines are equal (AF = AB = BE = FE = BC = CD = ED).
Draw AF = 4 cm.
Draw a line perpendicular to AF at A. With the compass tip at A and radius AF, mark B on this line.
Keep the same radius and mark C beyond B so that BC = AF.
Do the same at F to place the other corners and complete the rectangle ACDF.
items.answer: AC = 8 cm. The rectangle is 8 cm by 4 cm.

videos.answer: AC = 8 cm. The rectangle is 8 cm by 4 cm.

source: Construct a rectangle that can be divided into 3 identical s

items.question: Construct a rectangle that can be divided into 3 identical squares (a rectangle split by two vertical lines into three equal squares).
steps: Choose the square side, say 3 cm.
Draw a rough diagram showing 3 equal squares side by side.
Draw AB = 3 cm, draw perpendiculars at A and B, and mark AD = 3 cm and BC = 3 cm.
Use the compass to transfer the 3 cm length along the line two more times so that the total length is 9 cm.
Draw the dividing lines to check each part is a 3 cm square.
items.answer: Any rectangle whose length is 3 times its breadth, for example 9 cm by 3 cm. Each square has side 3 cm.

videos.answer: Any rectangle whose length is 3 times its breadth, for example 9 cm by 3 cm. Each square has side 3 cm.

source: Give the lengths of the sides of a rectangle that cannot be

items.question: Give the lengths of the sides of a rectangle that cannot be divided into two identical squares, and of a rectangle that cannot be divided into three identical squares. a) Cannot be divided into two identical squares b) Cannot be divided into three identical squares
steps: A rectangle splits into two identical squares only if length = 2 × breadth.
4 cm is not 2 × 2.5 cm.
It splits into three only if length = 3 × breadth; 7 cm is not 3 × 2 cm.
items.answer: a) for example 4 cm by 2.5 cm, b) for example 7 cm by 2 cm (other answers possible)

videos.answer: a) for example 4 cm by 2.5 cm, b) for example 7 cm by 2 cm (other answers possible)

source: Construct 1: A Square within a Rectangle (section 8.4)

items.question: Construct a rectangle of sides 8 cm and 4 cm. How will you construct a square inside, as shown in the figure, such that the centre of the square is the same as the centre of the rectangle? (The square touches the top and bottom of the rectangle and sits in the middle of its length.)
steps: Draw the 8 cm by 4 cm rectangle.
The square must fit between top and bottom, so its side is 4 cm.
Leave (8 cm − 4 cm) ÷ 2 = 2 cm on each side.
Mark points 2 cm in from each short side and draw the vertical lines of the square.
items.answer: The square has side 4 cm. Its left and right sides are 2 cm away from the left and right sides of the rectangle.

videos.answer: The square has side 4 cm. Its left and right sides are 2 cm away from the left and right sides of the rectangle.

steps: Draw the square.
Draw both diagonals; they meet at the centre.
Put the compass tip at that point and draw a circle inside the square.
items.answer: The centre of the circle should be at the meeting point of the two diagonals of the square (the line segments joining opposite corners).

steps: Draw the first square of side 4 cm with perpendicular sides.
From its top right corner draw the next square of side 4 cm going up and right.
Repeat for the third.
For the second picture start with 7 cm, then 5 cm, then 3 cm.
items.answer: Open ended. A correct drawing: three 4 cm squares meeting corner to corner, and then squares of sides 7 cm, 5 cm and 3 cm meeting corner to corner in a staircase.

items.question: Construct the figure: a large square divided into smaller squares, some halved by diagonals with one half shaded with parallel lines, and a plain larger square in a corner. Choose measurements of your choice. The larger 4-sided figure is a square and so are the smaller ones.
steps: Choose the side of the small square, say 1 cm, and draw the large square of 4 cm by 4 cm.
Draw the grid lines using perpendiculars.
Draw the diagonals in the small squares.
Shade one triangle in each with parallel lines.
items.answer: Open ended. A correct drawing has a large square made of equal small squares (with one plain larger square covering a 2 by 2 block), with diagonals drawn and the same triangle of each small square shaded.

steps: Draw one square and its middle lines to form 4 equal squares.
Draw the diagonals of each small square to find its centre.
Draw a circle with the same radius at each centre.
items.answer: Open ended. A correct drawing has four equal squares, each with a circle of the same radius at its centre (the meeting point of its diagonals).

items.question: This is a square with 8 cm sidelengths. Construct it so that four arcs, one on each side, bulge uniformly inwards from each side, each arc going from one corner of its side to the other corner.
steps: Draw a square of side 8 cm.
Open the compass to 8 cm.
Put the tip at one end of a side and mark an arc outside the square; do the same from the other end; the two arcs cross at a point outside.
Put the tip at that crossing point and draw the arc from one corner to the other.
Repeat for the other three sides.
items.answer: Open ended. A correct drawing: a square of side 8 cm with four equal arcs bulging inward. For example, use radius 8 cm and place each compass tip outside the square at the point that is 8 cm from both ends of that side; each arc then dips about 1 cm into the square.

videos.answer: Open ended. A correct drawing: a square of side 8 cm with four equal arcs bulging inward. For example, use radius 8 cm and place each compass tip outside the square at the point that is 8 cm from both ends of that side; each arc then dips about 1 cm into the square.

source: Rectangle PQRS has diagonals PR and QS. Predict whether the

items.question: Rectangle PQRS has diagonals PR and QS. Predict whether the two diagonals are equal in length, then construct a rectangle (for example 6 cm by 4 cm) and measure both diagonals. What do you find?
steps: Draw a rectangle PQRS, for example 6 cm long and 4 cm wide, using the ruler and set square or compass.
Join P to R and Q to S.
Measure PR and QS with the ruler.
Both measure about 7.2 cm, so the diagonals are equal.
Try another rectangle: the diagonals are equal again.
items.answer: The two diagonals are equal in length. For a 6 cm by 4 cm rectangle each diagonal is about 7.2 cm.

videos.answer: The two diagonals are equal in length. For a 6 cm by 4 cm rectangle each diagonal is about 7.2 cm.

source: In rectangle PQRS the diagonal PR divides angle R into g and

items.question: In rectangle PQRS the diagonal PR divides angle R into g and h, and divides angle P into c and d. Predict, then measure: are g and h equal? Are c and d equal? a) Are g and h equal? b) Are c and d equal?
steps: Draw a rectangle that is not a square, for example 6 cm by 4 cm, and its diagonal PR.
Measure c, d at P and g, h at R with a protractor.
For 6 cm by 4 cm the angles are about 34° and 56°, so c and d differ.
In a square both angles are 45°.
In each case the two small angles add up to 90°.
items.answer: a) g and h are not equal unless the rectangle is a square; b) c and d are not equal unless the rectangle is a square. In every rectangle g + h = 90° and c + d = 90°.

videos.answer: a) g and h are not equal unless the rectangle is a square; b) c and d are not equal unless the rectangle is a square. In every rectangle g + h = 90° and c + d = 90°.

source: In rectangle PQRS, with both diagonals drawn, the eight angl

items.question: In rectangle PQRS, with both diagonals drawn, the eight angles formed by the diagonals and the sides are a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h (at P: c and d; at Q: e and f; at R: g and h; at S: a and b; c is next to side PS, d next to PQ, e next to QP, f next to QR, g next to RQ, h next to RS, a next to SR, b next to SP). Measure them. Which angles are equal?
steps: Draw a rectangle that is not a square and both its diagonals.
Measure all eight angles with a protractor.
The four angles next to the long sides come out equal: d, e, a, h.
The four angles next to the short sides come out equal: c, f, g, b.
Each pair from the two groups adds up to 90°.
items.answer: d = e = a = h (the four angles next to the sides PQ and SR) and c = f = g = b (the four angles next to the sides PS and QR). Also c + d = 90°.

videos.answer: d = e = a = h (the four angles next to the sides PQ and SR) and c = f = g = b (the four angles next to the sides PS and QR). Also c + d = 90°.

source: How should the rectangle be constructed so that the diagonal

items.question: How should the rectangle be constructed so that the diagonal divides the opposite angles into equal parts?
steps: Try rectangles whose sides are different: the diagonal splits the right angle into unequal parts.
Make the adjacent sides equal, for example 5 cm and 5 cm.
Draw the diagonal and measure: both parts are 45°.
So only a square works.
items.answer: The two adjacent sides must be equal, that is, the rectangle must be a square. Then each diagonal divides the opposite angles into 45° and 45°.

videos.answer: The two adjacent sides must be equal, that is, the rectangle must be a square. Then each diagonal divides the opposite angles into 45° and 45°.

source: In your experiment, consider the case when all four sides of

items.question: In your experiment, consider the case when all four sides of the rectangle are equal, that is, a square. Draw a square (for example with side 5 cm), draw both diagonals, and see what happens.
steps: Draw a square of side 5 cm.
Join both diagonals.
Measure the eight angles with a protractor: each is 45°.
Measure the diagonals: both are about 7.1 cm.
items.answer: In a square each diagonal divides the opposite angles into 45° and 45°. All eight angles formed by the diagonals and the sides are 45°, and the two diagonals are equal (about 7.1 cm for a 5 cm square).

videos.answer: In a square each diagonal divides the opposite angles into 45° and 45°. All eight angles formed by the diagonals and the sides are 45°, and the two diagonals are equal (about 7.1 cm for a 5 cm square).

source: Math Talk (section 8.5): general laws

items.question: What general laws did you observe with respect to the angles and sides of a rectangle and its diagonals? Try to frame them.
steps: Look at your table of sides and the eight angles for several rectangles.
Notice which numbers repeat in each row.
Write each repeated pattern as a rule.
Check the special case of a square separately.
items.answer: In every rectangle: opposite sides are equal and all angles are 90°; the two diagonals are equal in length (and cut each other into equal halves); each diagonal divides the opposite angles into two angles that add up to 90°; the angles the diagonals make with the sides are equal in pairs (d = e = a = h and c = f = g = b). If the adjacent sides are equal (a square), each diagonal divides the opposite angles into 45° and 45°; if not, the two parts are unequal.

videos.answer: In every rectangle: opposite sides are equal and all angles are 90°; the two diagonals are equal in length (and cut each other into equal halves); each diagonal divides the opposite angles into two angles that add up to 90°; the angles the diagonals make with the sides are equal in pairs (d = e = a = h and c = f = g = b). If the adjacent sides are equal (a square), each diagonal divides the opposite angles into 45° and 45°; if not, the two parts are unequal.

source: Math Talk (section 8.5): will the laws always be true

items.question: How can one be sure that the laws you have observed will always be true?
steps: Try many different rectangles and see if the law holds each time.
Notice that measurements are only close, not exact.
Look for a reason using properties already known, for example that opposite sides are parallel.
A reason that works for every rectangle makes us sure.
items.answer: Measuring a few examples cannot prove a law for every rectangle, because measurements are approximate and we cannot try all rectangles. We need a reason that works for any rectangle, such as using what we know (opposite sides equal, all angles 90°, alternate angles at parallel sides) to explain why the pattern must hold.

videos.answer: Measuring a few examples cannot prove a law for every rectangle, because measurements are approximate and we cannot try all rectangles. We need a reason that works for any rectangle, such as using what we know (opposite sides equal, all angles 90°, alternate angles at parallel sides) to explain why the pattern must hold.

source: Construct a rectangle in which one of the diagonals divides

items.question: Construct a rectangle in which one of the diagonals divides the opposite angles into 60° and 30°.
steps: Draw AB of any length. At B draw a perpendicular line (90°).
At A use the protractor to draw a 60° angle with AB. Where this ray meets the perpendicular from B, mark C.
Through A draw a line perpendicular to AB. This is the line on which D lies, and angle A is now 60° + 30°.
Find D. Method 1: draw a perpendicular to BC at C, and D is where it meets the line through A. Method 2: with the compass take length BC and mark D on the line through A so that AD = BC.
Join CD. ABCD is the rectangle. Check: AB = CD, AD = BC and every angle is 90°.
items.answer: Rectangle ABCD in which the diagonal AC makes 60° with side AB and 30° with side AD (angle A = 90° = 60° + 30°). The side lengths can be chosen freely, as only the angles are given.

videos.answer: Rectangle ABCD in which the diagonal AC makes 60° with side AB and 30° with side AD (angle A = 90° = 60° + 30°). The side lengths can be chosen freely, as only the angles are given.

source: Angle A of the rectangle is divided by the diagonal into two

items.question: Angle A of the rectangle is divided by the diagonal into two angles. One measures 60°. Check what the other angle is.
steps: Angle A of a rectangle is 90°.
The two parts add up to 90°.
Check with a protractor: the other angle measures 30°.

source: Construct Q1 (section 8.5)

items.question: Construct a rectangle in which one of the diagonals divides the opposite angles into 50° and 40°.
steps: Draw AB of any length. At B draw a perpendicular (90°).
At A draw a 50° angle with AB. The ray meets the perpendicular from B at C.
Draw the perpendicular to AB at A. Then the other angle at A is 90° − 50° = 40°.
Draw a perpendicular to BC at C. It meets the line through A at D.
Check: AB = CD, AD = BC, all angles 90°.
items.answer: Rectangle ABCD in which the diagonal AC makes 50° with side AB and 40° with side AD (at C the diagonal makes 50° with CD and 40° with CB). Side lengths are free.

videos.answer: Rectangle ABCD in which the diagonal AC makes 50° with side AB and 40° with side AD (at C the diagonal makes 50° with CD and 40° with CB). Side lengths are free.

source: Construct Q2 (section 8.5)

items.question: Construct a rectangle in which one of the diagonals divides the opposite angles into 45° and 45°. What do you observe about the sides? a) Construct the rectangle. b) What do you observe about the sides?
steps: Draw AB of any length. At B draw a perpendicular.
At A draw a 45° angle with AB. It meets the perpendicular at C.
Draw the perpendicular to AB at A (the other angle at A is 90° − 45° = 45°).
Draw the perpendicular to BC at C. It meets the line through A at D.
Measure the sides: AB = BC = CD = DA. It is a square.
items.answer: a) the rectangle is built with 45° at A next to AB and 45° next to AD; b) all the sides are equal, so it is a square.

videos.answer: a) the rectangle is built with 45° at A next to AB and 45° next to AD; b) all the sides are equal, so it is a square.

source: Construct a rectangle where one of its sides is 5 cm and the

items.question: Construct a rectangle where one of its sides is 5 cm and the length of a diagonal is 7 cm.
steps: Draw base DC = 5 cm.
At C draw a line l perpendicular to DC (90°).
With the compass opened to 7 cm and centre D, draw an arc that cuts line l. The cutting point is B (DB = 7 cm).
Draw a perpendicular to DC at D and a perpendicular to BC at B. They meet at A. (Or mark A with the compass so that DA = CB and AB = DC.)
Check: AB = 5 cm, BC = AD, angles 90°, diagonal DB = 7 cm.
items.answer: Rectangle ABCD with DC = AB = 5 cm and diagonal DB = 7 cm. The other two sides AD = BC come out about 4.9 cm and all four angles are 90°.

videos.answer: Rectangle ABCD with DC = AB = 5 cm and diagonal DB = 7 cm. The other two sides AD = BC come out about 4.9 cm and all four angles are 90°.

items.question: To construct the rectangle with a side of 5 cm and a diagonal of 7 cm, which line can be drawn first?
steps: Only one length that is a side is known: 5 cm.
Draw this side first as the base CD.

items.answer: The base CD, which is 5 cm long.

items.question: Line l is perpendicular to DC at C, and the point B must lie on l. What else do we know about the position of B?
steps: The diagonal DB = 7 cm.
So B is 7 cm from D.
B is also on line l.
B is the point of l that is 7 cm from D.
items.answer: B is at a distance of 7 cm from the point D (since the diagonal DB is 7 cm).

videos.answer: B is at a distance of 7 cm from the point D (since the diagonal DB is 7 cm).

source: A circle of radius 7 cm is drawn with centre D, and it meets

items.question: A circle of radius 7 cm is drawn with centre D, and it meets line l at a point. What is the distance of that point from D?
steps: Every point of a circle is at the radius distance from the centre.
The radius is 7 cm.
So the point where the circle meets l is 7 cm from D, and it is B.
items.answer: 7 cm. This point is the required point B.

steps: Measure AB and DC with a ruler: both 5 cm.

source: Construct Q3 (section 8.5)

items.question: Construct a rectangle one of whose sides is 4 cm and the diagonal is of length 8 cm.
steps: Draw PQ = 4 cm.
At P draw a perpendicular line.
With the compass opened to 8 cm and centre Q, draw an arc cutting this perpendicular at S (QS = 8 cm).
Draw a perpendicular to PQ at Q and a line through S parallel to PQ (perpendicular to PS). They meet at R.
Check: PQ = SR = 4 cm, PS = QR, angles 90°, diagonal QS = 8 cm.
items.answer: Rectangle PQRS with PQ = SR = 4 cm and diagonal QS = 8 cm. The other sides PS = QR are about 6.9 cm.

videos.answer: Rectangle PQRS with PQ = SR = 4 cm and diagonal QS = 8 cm. The other sides PS = QR are about 6.9 cm.

source: Construct Q4 (section 8.5)

items.question: Construct a rectangle one of whose sides is 3 cm and the diagonal is of length 7 cm.
steps: Draw AB = 3 cm.
At A draw a perpendicular line.
With the compass opened to 7 cm and centre B, draw an arc cutting this perpendicular at D (BD = 7 cm).
Draw a perpendicular to AB at B and a line through D perpendicular to AD. They meet at C.
Check: AB = DC = 3 cm, AD = BC, angles 90°, diagonal BD = 7 cm.
items.answer: Rectangle ABCD with AB = DC = 3 cm and diagonal BD = 7 cm. The other sides AD = BC are about 6.3 cm.

videos.answer: Rectangle ABCD with AB = DC = 3 cm and diagonal BD = 7 cm. The other sides AD = BC are about 6.3 cm.

source: The two circles of radius 5 cm centred at B and at C meet at

items.question: The two circles of radius 5 cm centred at B and at C meet at a point (the apex A). How far is that point from B? How far is it from C? a) Distance from B b) Distance from C
steps: The point lies on the circle centred at B with radius 5 cm.
So it is 5 cm from B.
It also lies on the circle centred at C with radius 5 cm, so it is 5 cm from C.
This is the apex A.
items.answer: a) 5 cm, b) 5 cm. So it is the point A.

videos.answer: a) 5 cm, b) 5 cm. So it is the point A.

source: Was it necessary to draw two full circles to get the point A

items.question: Was it necessary to draw two full circles to get the point A?
steps: The point A is where the two circles cross.
Only the small parts near the crossing matter.
Draw just arcs from B and from C with 5 cm radius.
Where they cross is A.
items.answer: No. Only a part of each circle is needed, so short arcs of radius 5 cm from B and from C that cross at A are enough.

videos.answer: No. Only a part of each circle is needed, so short arcs of radius 5 cm from B and from C that cross at A are enough.

source: Recreate this house figure. All the lines forming the border

items.question: Recreate this house figure. All the lines forming the border of the house are of length 5 cm. The house has a rectangular part with base DE = 5 cm and vertical sides DB = 5 cm and EC = 5 cm, a door 1 cm wide and 2 cm tall on the base, a roof with sides AB = 5 cm and AC = 5 cm meeting at the top point A, and a curved arc from B to C.
steps: Draw base DE = 5 cm. Draw perpendiculars at D and E and mark B and C each 5 cm up. Draw the door, 1 cm wide and 2 cm tall, on DE.
To find A, which is 5 cm from both B and C: set the compass to 5 cm and draw an arc from B (the circle of all points 5 cm from B).
With the same 5 cm opening draw an arc from C. The two arcs meet at A, which is 5 cm from B and 5 cm from C. Join AB and AC.
With the compass at A and radius 5 cm, draw the arc from B to C (it bulges down into the house).
Check AB = AC = 5 cm.
items.answer: A house with DE = DB = EC = AB = AC = 5 cm, a door 1 cm wide and 2 cm tall on the base, apex A found as the point 5 cm from both B and C, and an arc from B to C drawn with centre A and radius 5 cm. Since BC = 5 cm as well, triangle ABC has all sides 5 cm.

videos.answer: A house with DE = DB = EC = AB = AC = 5 cm, a door 1 cm wide and 2 cm tall on the base, apex A found as the point 5 cm from both B and C, and an arc from B to C drawn with centre A and radius 5 cm. Since BC = 5 cm as well, triangle ABC has all sides 5 cm.

source: Construct Q1 (section 8.6)

items.question: Construct a bigger house in which all the sides are of length 7 cm.
steps: Draw DE = 7 cm, then perpendiculars at D and E; mark B and C 7 cm above D and E.
Draw a door on DE (the book's solution uses 2 cm wide and 3 cm tall).
With the compass at 7 cm, draw arcs from B and from C. They meet at A. Join AB and AC.
With the compass at A and radius 7 cm, draw the arc from B to C.
Check: every border line is 7 cm.
items.answer: A house like the earlier one with all border lines 7 cm: DE = DB = EC = AB = AC = 7 cm, apex A 7 cm from B and from C, and an arc BC with centre A and radius 7 cm. The book's solution draws a door 2 cm wide and 3 cm tall.

videos.answer: A house like the earlier one with all border lines 7 cm: DE = DB = EC = AB = AC = 7 cm, apex A 7 cm from B and from C, and an arc BC with centre A and radius 7 cm. The book's solution draws a door 2 cm wide and 3 cm tall.

source: Construct Q2 (section 8.6)

items.question: Try to recreate ‘A Person’, ‘Wavy Wave’, and ‘Eyes’ from the section ‘Artwork’, using ideas involved in the ‘House’ construction.
steps: Person: draw a circle with the compass for the head, then a neck line and a square for the body.
Wave: mark equal parts on a central line and draw half circles with the compass, one above and the next below.
Eyes: draw a light horizontal line. From a point A above it draw the lower curve, and from a point B below it draw the upper curve, with the same compass opening, so the two arcs meet at the ends.
Place A and B symmetrically (same distance from the line) so the eye is symmetrical.
Copy the eye for the second one and add the pupils.
items.answer: Open drawing. A correct drawing shows: A Person (a circle for the head, for example radius 2 cm, a short neck line, and a 4 cm by 4 cm square body in the book's solution); Wavy Wave (equal half circles drawn alternately above and below a central line); Eyes (two matching lens-shaped eyes, each made from an upper and a lower arc drawn from compass points A above and B below, placed symmetrically, with a filled round pupil).

videos.answer: Open drawing. A correct drawing shows: A Person (a circle for the head, for example radius 2 cm, a short neck line, and a 4 cm by 4 cm square body in the book's solution); Wavy Wave (equal half circles drawn alternately above and below a central line); Eyes (two matching lens-shaped eyes, each made from an upper and a lower arc drawn from compass points A above and B below, placed symmetrically, with a filled round pupil).

source: Construct Q3 (section 8.6)

items.question: Is there a 4-sided figure in which all the sides are equal in length but is not a square? If such a figure exists, can you construct it? a) Does such a figure exist? b) Can you construct it?
steps: Take side length 5 cm. Draw AB = 5 cm and AC = 5 cm with angle A not equal to 90°, for example 60°.
The fourth point D must be 5 cm from both B and C.
With the compass at 5 cm, draw an arc from B and an arc from C. They cross at D.
Join BD and CD. All four sides AB, AC, BD, CD are 5 cm.
The angles are not 90°, so it is not a square.
items.answer: a) Yes, a rhombus (diamond) with four equal sides and angles that are not 90°; b) yes, it can be constructed with compass arcs.

videos.answer: a) Yes, a rhombus (diamond) with four equal sides and angles that are not 90°; b) yes, it can be constructed with compass arcs.
